Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe state of the church is represented under the figure of a temple measured.1, 2Two witnesses prophesy is sackcloth.3–6They are slain, after which they arise and ascend to heaven.7–13Under the seventh trumpet, all antichristian powers are to be destroyed and there will be a glorious state of Christ's kingdom upon earth.14–19
God's temple and its worshipers are measured (verses 1 and 2)

The symbolic measuring of the temple seems to recall Ezekiel's vision.

Henry proposes several possible purposes: preserving the church during public danger, testing its condition, or reforming it.

God's people must be examined to see whether they pursue his glory as the purpose of worship and follow his word as the rule for everything they do.

Those remaining in the outer court picture people who worship wrongly or pretend to have sincere hearts; their hypocrisy will eventually be exposed.

God will preserve a temple and an altar—true worship—somewhere in this world until the end of time.

He carefully watches over his church.

The holy city represents the visible church.

It may be trampled and filled with idolaters, unbelievers and hypocrites, but its period of devastation is limited.

The Lord will ultimately rescue his people from their troubles.

The witnesses suffer and are restored (verses 3–13)

During periods when the church was oppressed, God maintained faithful witnesses to declare the truth of his word and worship and the goodness of his ways.

They were few, yet enough to accomplish the task.

They prophesied in sackcloth, signifying both the persecution and hardship they endured and their grief at the sins against which they testified.

God sustained them through their long and difficult service until their assigned work was complete.

Henry interprets the 1,260 years as an extended period of testimony during which Antichrist, understood as a great instrument of Satan, would eventually attack the witnesses with force.

He believed the witnesses' final suffering and restoration were probably still future in his own time.

He also acknowledged that Christians might again endure severe outward persecution, and that there was already abundant reason to mourn the state of religion.

He suggested that the depressed condition described could refer particularly to the Western church.

These are Henry's historically situated proposals about prophetic fulfillment, not dates or identifications certain from the biblical text.

People hardened against divine truth rejoice when they manage to silence, banish or kill faithful witnesses, because the witnesses' teaching and conduct trouble their consciences.

But the Spirit of life from God revives the spiritually dead.

He will restore his people and renew the church's seemingly dying witness.

Such revival terrifies its enemies.

Where there is guilt, there is fear; a persecuting spirit can be cruel but remains cowardly.

The vindication and public honor of those who suffered for God will itself be part of the judgment against their persecutors, both in this world and at the last day.

Christ's witnesses must not grow tired of serving or suffering, nor impatiently seize a reward before its time.

They must wait until their Master calls them.

The revival and exaltation of the witnesses brings a mighty upheaval to their opponents' dominion.

Henry cautions that events alone will disclose the precise meaning of those prophecies.

But the broader principle is clear: when God's work and witnesses revive, Satan's work is defeated.

The seventh trumpet and God's kingdom (verses 14–19)

Before the seventh and final trumpet, a solemn announcement demands attention.

The saints and angels in heaven recognize God's and the Savior's right to rule the entire world.

But the nations answer God's righteous anger with their own rebellion.

The Lord begins rewarding his people's faithful work and suffering.

His enemies become more hostile and thereby increase their own guilt and hasten judgment.

The opening of God's heavenly temple might picture freer fellowship between heaven and earth: more frequent prayer and praise rising to God and blessings descending.

Henry nevertheless considers it more likely that the image represents changes in the church on earth.

During what he calls Antichrist's reign, God's law was set aside in favor of human traditions and decrees, and Scripture was withheld from ordinary people.

Now God's word is brought openly before everyone.

The ark's reappearance then symbolizes God's returning presence and favor through Jesus Christ, the atoning sacrifice for sins.

Henry relates this to the Protestant Reformation and the extraordinary events surrounding it.

The God who heard prayer answered it through mighty acts of righteousness.
classic_reading:
[Rev.11.1-Rev.11.2]
Chapter 11
Chapter Outline
The state of the church is represented under the figure of a temple measured.
(1-2)
Two witnesses prophesy is sackcloth.
(3-6)
They are slain, after which they arise and ascend to heaven.
(7-13)
Under the seventh trumpet, all antichristian powers are to be destroyed and there will be a glorious state of Christ's kingdom upon earth.
(14-19)
Verses 1-2
This prophetical passage about measuring the temple seems to refer to Ezekiel's vision. The design of this measuring seems to be the preservation of the church in times of public danger; or for its trial, or for its reformation. The worshippers must be measured; whether they make God's glory their end, and his word their rule, in all their acts of worship. Those in the outer court, worship in a false manner, or with dissembling hearts, and will be found among his enemies. God will have a temple and an altar in the world, till the end of time. He looks strictly to his temple. The holy city, the visible church, is trodden under foot; is filled with idolaters, infidels, and hypocrites. But the desolations of the church are limited, and she shall be delivered out of all her troubles.
[Rev.11.3-Rev.11.13]
Verses 3-13
In the time of treading down, God kept his faithful witnesses to attest the truth of his word and worship, and the excellence of his ways, The number of these witnesses is small, yet enough. They prophesy in sackcloth. It shows their afflicted, persecuted state, and deep sorrow for the abominations against which they protested. They are supported during their great and hard work, till it is done. When they had prophesied in sackcloth the greatest part of 1260 years, antichrist, the great instrument of the devil, would war against them, with force and violence for a time. Determined rebels against the light rejoice, as on some happy event, when they can silence, drive to a distance, or destroy the faithful servants of Christ, whose doctrine and conduct torment them. It does not appear that the term is yet expired, and the witnesses are not a present exposed to endure such terrible outward sufferings as in former times; but such things may again happen, and there is abundant cause to prophesy in sackcloth, on account of the state of religion. The depressed state of real Christianity may relate only to the western church. The Spirit of life from God, quickens dead souls, and shall quicken the dead bodies of his people, and his dying interest in the world. The revival of God's work and witnesses, will strike terror into the souls of his enemies. Where there is guilt, there is fear; and a persecuting spirit, though cruel, is a cowardly spirit. It will be no small part of the punishment of persecutors, both in this world, and at the great day, that they see the faithful servants of God honoured and advanced. The Lord's witnesses must not be weary of suffering and service, nor hastily grasp at the reward; but must stay till their Master calls them. The consequence of their being thus exalted was a mighty shock and convulsion in the antichristian empire. Events alone can show the meaning of this. But whenever God's work and witnesses revive, the devil's work and witnesses fall before him. And that the slaying of the witnesses is future, appears to be probable.
[Rev.11.14-Rev.11.19]
Verses 14-19
Before the sounding of the seventh and last trumpet, there is the usual demand of attention. The saints and angels in heaven know the right of our God and Saviour to rule over all the world. But the nations met God's wrath with their own anger. It was a time in which he was beginning to reward his people's faithful services, and sufferings; and their enemies fretted against God, and so increased their guilt, and hastened their destruction. By the opening the temple of God in heaven, may be meant, that there was a more free communication between heaven and earth; prayer and praises more freely and frequently going up, graces and blessings plentifully coming down. But it rather seems to refer to the church of God on earth. In the reign of antichrist, God's law was laid aside, and made void by traditions and decrees; the Scriptures were locked up from the people, but now they are brought to the view of all. This, like the ark, is a token of the presence of God returned to his people, and his favour toward them in Jesus Christ, as the Propitiation for their sins. The great blessing of the Reformation was attended with very awful providences; as by terrible things in righteousness God answered the prayers presented in his holy temple now opened.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesA description of the church of Christ and of Satan, under the figures of a woman and of a great red dragon.1–6Michael and his angels fight against the devil and his angels, who are defeated.7–12The dragon persecutes the church.13, 14His vain endeavours to destroy her, He renews his war against her seed.14–17
The woman and the dragon (verses 1–6)

John saw the church pictured as a woman in heaven, the mother of believers.

She was clothed with the sun, representing the way believers are justified, sanctified and made radiant through union with Christ, the Sun of Righteousness.

The moon beneath her feet showed her greater light compared with the reflected and weaker revelation received through Moses.

Her crown of twelve stars represented gospel teaching proclaimed by the twelve apostles, a glory belonging to all genuine believers.

She labored to bring forth a holy family, desiring that sinners' conviction would lead to their conversion.

The red dragon represents Satan and his chief agents—those who govern in his interests on earth.

Henry identifies this particular historical embodiment with the pagan Roman Empire, the city of seven hills.

He interprets the ten horns as ten kingdoms and the seven crowns as seven forms of government.

Those are his historical and symbolic interpretations, not settled facts supplied by the passage itself.

The dragon's tail sweeping away a third of the stars pictures the persecution and seduction of ministers and teachers.

The enemy sought to crush Christianity.

Nevertheless, the church brought forth a faithful and vigorous people in whom Christ was formed anew.

The Son of God will govern the nations, and his people share the honor he wins for them.

God protected this blessed offspring.

The dragon's defeat and the church's weapons (verses 7–11)

The dragon's attack upon the church ultimately damaged his own cause.

Henry understands the conflict in heaven as being fought in Christ's church, the kingdom of heaven present on earth.

He identifies the opposing sides with Christ, the great Angel of the covenant, and his faithful people, and Satan with his instruments.

The church's strength rests in having Jesus Christ as Captain of its salvation.

Henry connects the dragon's defeat with pagan idolatry being driven out of the Roman Empire through Christianity's spread.

The church owes its deliverance and strength entirely to its King and Head.

The devil hates God's presence, yet is willing to appear before him in order to accuse believers.

We must take care not to provide grounds for such accusations.

When we do sin, we should confess before God, condemn our own wrongdoing and entrust our case to Jesus Christ as Advocate.

God's people overcome Satan through three means.

First, the blood of the Lamb is the only foundation of their hope.

Second, their testimony to the gospel is powerful through God to bring down spiritual strongholds.

Third, they show courage and patience in suffering, loving Christ more than their own lives and being willing to die rather than abandon his cause.

Henry sees these as the instruments through which Christianity overcame pagan idolatry.

He argues that if Christians had continued to rely upon these spiritual weapons, instead of other means, their victories would have been greater, more lasting and more glorious.

We too must trust the Lamb's blood alone, without adding anything else as a basis for salvation.

The dragon persecutes the remaining faithful (verses 12–17)

Christ's church and its friends rightly praise God for deliverance from pagan persecution, although further trials await.

The wilderness is desolate and dangerous, inhabited by serpents and scorpions and lacking ordinary comforts.

Yet it can also be a place of refuge and safety.

Even withdrawal into such a refuge did not completely protect the woman from the dragon.

Henry records two proposed interpretations of the flood that the dragon sent against her.

Some understood it as the barbarian invasions that overwhelmed the Western Roman Empire, with pagan opponents hoping that the destruction would also end Christianity.

But people acting from worldly interests nevertheless protected the church through those upheavals, so the end of the empire did not secure a victory for idolatry.

Alternatively, the flood might mean a torrent of error threatening to sweep away God's people.

Neither identification is presented as certain.

Defeated in his attempts against the church as a whole, Satan turned his anger against particular believers and communities.

Faithfulness to God and Christ in teaching, worship and conduct exposes Christians to spiritual opposition.

That conflict continues until the final enemy is destroyed.
classic_reading:
[Rev.12.1-Rev.12.6]
Chapter 12
Chapter Outline
A description of the church of Christ and of Satan, under the figures of a woman and of a great red dragon.
(1-6)
Michael and his angels fight against the devil and his angels, who are defeated.
(7-12)
The dragon persecutes the church.
(13-14)
His vain endeavours to destroy her, He renews his war against her seed.
(14-17)
Verses 1-6
The church, under the emblem of a woman, the mother of believers, was seen by the apostle in vision, in heaven. She was clothed with the sun, justified, sanctified, and shining by union with Christ, the Sun of Righteousness. The moon was under her feet; she was superior to the reflected and feebler light of the revelation made by Moses. Having on her head a crown of twelve stars; the doctrine of the gospel, preached by the twelve apostles, is a crown of glory to all true believers. As in pain to bring forth a holy family; desirous that the conviction of sinners might end in their conversion. A dragon is a known emblem of Satan, and his chief agents, or those who govern for him on earth, at that time the pagan empire of Rome, the city built upon seven hills. As having ten horns, divided into ten kingdoms. Having seven crowns, representing seven forms of government. As drawing with his tail a third part of the stars in heaven, and casting them down to the earth; persecuting and seducing the ministers and teachers. As watchful to crush the Christian religion; but in spite of the opposition of enemies, the church brought forth a manly issue of true and faithful professors, in whom Christ was truly formed anew; even the mystery of Christ, that Son of God who should rule the nations, and in whose right his members partake the same glory. This blessed offspring was protected of God.
[Rev.12.7-Rev.12.11]
Verses 7-11
The attempts of the dragon proved unsuccessful against the church, and fatal to his own interests. The seat of this war was in heaven; in the church of Christ, the kingdom of heaven on earth. The parties were Christ, the great Angel of the covenant, and his faithful followers; and Satan and his instruments. The strength of the church is in having the Lord Jesus for the Captain of their salvation. Pagan idolatry, which was the worship of devils, was cast out of the empire by the spreading of Christianity. The salvation and strength of the church, are only to be ascribed to the King and Head of the church. The conquered enemy hates the presence of God, yet he is willing to appear there, to accuse the people of God. Let us take heed that we give him no cause to accuse us; and that, when we have sinned, we go before the Lord, condemn ourselves, and commit our cause to Christ as our Advocate. The servants of God overcame Satan by the blood of the Lamb, as the cause. By the word of their testimony: the powerful preaching of the gospel is mighty, through God, to pull down strong holds. By their courage and patience in sufferings: they loved not their lives so well but they could lay them down in Christ's cause. These were the warriors and the weapons by which Christianity overthrew the power of pagan idolatry; and if Christians had continued to fight with these weapons, and such as these, their victories would have been more numerous and glorious, and the effects more lasting. The redeemed overcame by a simple reliance on the blood of Christ, as the only ground of their hopes. In this we must be like them. We must not blend any thing else with this.
[Rev.12.12-Rev.12.17]
Verses 12-17
The church and all her friends might well be called to praise God for deliverance from pagan persecution, though other troubles awaited her. The wilderness is a desolate place, and full of serpents and scorpions, uncomfortable and destitute of provisions; yet a place of safety, as well as where one might be alone. But being thus retired could not protect the woman. The flood of water is explained by many to mean the invasions of barbarians, by which the western empire was overwhelmed; for the heathen encouraged their attacks, in the hope of destroying Christianity. But ungodly men, for their worldly interests, protected the church amidst these tumults, and the overthrow of the empire did not help the cause of idolatry. Or, this may be meant of a flood of error, by which the church of God was in danger of being overwhelmed and carried away. The devil, defeated in his designs upon the church, turns his rage against persons and places. Being faithful to God and Christ, in doctrine, worship, and practice, exposes to the rage of Satan; and will do so till the last enemy shall be destroyed.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesA wild beast rises out of the sea, to whom the dragon gives his power.1–10Another beast, which has two horns like a lamb, but speaks as a dragon.11–15It obliges all to worship its image, and receive its mark, as persons devoted to it.16–18
The first beast and its persecuting authority (verses 1–10)

John saw a terrifying beast rising from the sea.

Henry understands it as a tyrannical, idolatrous and persecuting power emerging from great public disturbances.

He connects it with worldly empires that had oppressed God's people for centuries, beginning as far back as the Babylonian captivity.

He particularly relates the fourth beast of Daniel's prophecy to the Roman Empire, under which many believers suffered cruel persecution.

The dragon—Satan—supplied the beast's authority and supported its power.

The wounded head may, in Henry's interpretation, signify the overthrow of Roman pagan idolatry.

Its healing may symbolize what Henry polemically called “popish idolatry”, a revived form of the same spiritual evil under a different outward appearance.

This reflects Henry's historical Protestant interpretation, not a fact or identity demonstrated beyond dispute by Revelation 13.

The world admired the beast's power, strategy and success.

People gave honor and obedience to the devil's instruments, granting creatures reverence that belongs to God alone.

Yet Satan's authority and his apparent success remain strictly limited.

Christ has a chosen remnant, redeemed by his blood, recorded in his book and sealed by his Spirit.

The beast and its allies may conquer the body and take away physical life, but cannot conquer the souls of genuine believers or make them finally abandon their Savior and join his enemies.

Those whose names are written in the book of life are characterized by endurance in gospel faith and faithful worship of God during severe temptation.

Encouraging this steadfastness is, Henry says, the principal design of the whole book of Revelation.

The second beast, enforced worship and the number 666 (verses 11–18)

Those who see the first beast as a form of worldly power interpret the second as another oppressive authority—a spiritual power disguising itself as true religion and concern for people's souls.

It presents itself as derived from Christ, and initially appears gentle.

But it soon speaks like the dragon.

Its false teaching and harsh commands reveal, in Henry's understanding, that it serves Satan rather than the Lamb.

It exercises the first beast's authority for the same end: drawing people away from the worship of the true God and placing human consciences under human control.

Henry describes deceptive signs and supposed miracles as instruments used to persuade people to worship the image of the earlier persecuting power.

Harsh censures are another means.

Those refusing its worship may be deprived of ordinary civil rights, opportunities to buy or sell, and positions of profit or trust.

Receiving its mark signifies binding oneself to advance its cause with all one's influence, strength and efforts.

To make the beast's image is to establish a form of its worship and authority.

To worship that image is to submit to the defining practices of the power it represents.

The beast's number is 666.

It invites the exercise of human wisdom while displaying the far greater wisdom of God.

But Henry says explicitly that the intended person or institution remains a mystery.

The number has been applied to nearly every religious controversy.

He even considers it reasonable to doubt whether its true meaning had yet been discovered.

What the believer can understand is that every enemy of God is known and numbered.

Their power has a limit, and their appointed end will come.

All nations will finally submit to the King of righteousness and peace.
classic_reading:
[Rev.13.1-Rev.13.10]
Chapter 13
Chapter Outline
A wild beast rises out of the sea, to whom the dragon gives his power.
(1-10)
Another beast, which has two horns like a lamb, but speaks as a dragon.
(11-15)
It obliges all to worship its image, and receive its mark, as persons devoted to it.
(16-18)
Verses 1-10
The apostle, standing on the shore, saw a savage beast rise out of the sea; a tyrannical, idolatrous, persecuting power, springing up out of the troubles which took place. It was a frightful monster! It appears to mean that worldly, oppressing dominion, which for many ages, even from the times of the Babylonish captivity, had been hostile to the church. The first beast then began to oppress and persecute the righteous for righteousness' sake, but they suffered most under the fourth beast of Daniel, (the Roman empire,) which has afflicted the saints with many cruel persecutions. The source of its power was the dragon. It was set up by the devil, and supported by him. The wounding the head may be the abolishing pagan idolatry; and the healing of the wound, introducing popish idolatry, the same in substance, only in a new dress, but which as effectually answers the devil's design. The world admired its power, policy and success. They paid honour and subjection to the devil and his instruments. It exercised infernal power and policy, requiring men to render that honour to creatures which belongs to God alone. Yet the devil's power and success are limited. Christ has a chosen remnant, redeemed by his blood, recorded in his book, sealed by his Spirit; and though the devil and antichrist may overcome the body, and take away the natural life, they cannot conquer the soul, nor prevail with true believers to forsake their Saviour, and join his enemies. Perseverance in the faith of the gospel and true worship of God, in this great hour of trial and temptation, which would deceive all but the elect, is the character of those registered in the book of life. This powerful motive and encouragement to constancy, is the great design of the whole Revelation.
[Rev.13.11-Rev.13.18]
Verses 11-18
Those who understand the first beast to denote a worldly power, take the second to be also a persecuting and assumed power, which acts under the disguise of religion, and of charity to the souls of men. It is a spiritual dominion, professing to be derived from Christ, and exercised at first in a gentle manner, but soon spake like the dragon. Its speech betrayed it; for it gives forth those false doctrines and cruel decrees, which show it to belong to the dragon, and not to the Lamb. It exercised all the power of the former beast. It pursues the same design, to draw men from worshipping the true God, and to subject the souls of men to the will and control of men. The second beast has carried on its designs, by methods whereby men should be deceived to worship the former beast, in the new shape, or likeness made for it. By lying wonders, pretended miracles. And by severe censures. Also by allowing none to enjoy natural or civil rights, who will not worship that beast which is the image of the pagan beast. It is made a qualification for buying and selling, as well as for places of profit and trust, that they oblige themselves to use all their interest, power, and endeavour, to forward the dominion of the beast, which is meant by receiving his mark. To make an image to the beast, whose deadly wound was healed, would be to give form and power to his worship, or to require obedience to his commands. To worship the image of the beast, implies being subject to those things which stamp the character of the picture, and render it the image of the beast. The number of the beast is given, so as to show the infinite wisdom of God, and to exercise the wisdom of men. The number is the number of a man, computed after the usual manner among men, and it is 666. What or who is intended by this, remains a mystery. To almost every religious dispute this number has yet been applied, and it may reasonably be doubted whether the meaning has yet been discovered. But he who has wisdom and understanding, will see that all the enemies of God are numbered and marked out for destruction; that the term of their power will soon expire, and that all nations shall submit to our King of righteousness and peace.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThose faithful to Christ celebrate the praises of God.1–5Three angels; one proclaiming the everlasting gospel; another, the downfal of Babylon; and a third, the dreadful wrath of God on the worshippers of the beast. The blessedness of those who die in the Lord.6–13A vision of Christ with a sickle, and of a harvest ripe for cutting down.14–16The emblem of a vintage fully ripe, trodden in the wine-press of God's wrath.17–20
The Lamb and his faithful people on Mount Zion (verses 1–5)

Mount Zion represents Christ's gospel church.

Jesus remains with her even amid all her troubles.

His presence protects the church from destruction and secures the perseverance of his people.

They appear with honor.

God's name written upon their foreheads shows that they openly and boldly confess faith in God and Jesus Christ, and then live in a way consistent with that confession.

Even in the darkest periods, some believers have been willing to suffer and die for the truth and worship of Christ's gospel.

They kept themselves from the wicked practices of those Henry identifies with Antichrist.

Their hearts were sincerely devoted to God.

They were freely forgiven in Christ, bringing glory to him and receiving glory in him.

Let our prayer, our labor and our ambition be to belong to that company.

The passage speaks about people truly justified and sanctified.

No hypocrite, however convincing an outward appearance may be, can be judged without fault before God.

The gospel proclaimed, Babylon warned and the faithful blessed (verses 6–13)

Henry suggests that this scene appears to describe the progress of the Protestant Reformation.

He sees the four proclamations or declarations in this passage as encouragement for Christians to remain faithful during testing.

This is his historical reading, not a prophetic date or identification independently established here.

The everlasting gospel is God's great means of bringing people to fear him and give him glory.

Its proclamation shakes the foundations of powers hostile to Christ and hastens their downfall.

Those who continue willingly serving the beast and promoting its cause, Henry warns, face misery of both soul and body forever.

Believers, by contrast, should be willing to endure hardship and loss while obeying God's commands and confessing their faith in Jesus.

May God grant us that patience.

Consider the blessedness of those who die in the Lord.

They die united to Christ and in the service of his cause; they belong to him when death comes.

They rest from sin, temptation, grief and persecution, where the wicked cease troubling them and the weary find repose.

Their works follow them.

Those works do not go before them as a price paid for salvation or a title by which to claim it.

They follow as evidence that these believers lived and died in Christ.

Remembering their service will bring joy, while their reward will far exceed any labor or suffering they endured.

The Holy Spirit assures them of this by his inward testimony and through the written word.

The harvest and the winepress (verses 14–20)

The warnings and earlier judgments have failed to bring universal repentance.

The wickedness of the nations reaches its full measure, so they become ripe for judgment.

The harvest can represent God's merciful gathering of righteous people into heaven when they are ready.

Grain is harvested when it has ripened.

In the same way, God's faithful people will be gathered into Christ's storehouse at the proper time.

The grape harvest and winepress, by contrast, represent judgment on Christ's enemies.

The Lord does not destroy them until their sins have ripened into complete guilt.

The winepress expresses the wrath of God in some dreadful calamity—Henry suggests probably the sword and bloodshed of the wicked.

God's patience toward sinners is an astonishing miracle.

But although his patience lasts a long time, it will not last forever.

When sin has reached its full measure, judgment is near.
classic_reading:
[Rev.14.1-Rev.14.5]
Chapter 14
Chapter Outline
Those faithful to Christ celebrate the praises of God.
(1-5)
Three angels; one proclaiming the everlasting gospel; another, the downfal of Babylon; and a third, the dreadful wrath of God on the worshippers of the beast. The blessedness of those who die in the Lord.
(6-13)
A vision of Christ with a sickle, and of a harvest ripe for cutting down.
(14-16)
The emblem of a vintage fully ripe, trodden in the wine-press of God's wrath.
(17-20)
Verses 1-5
Mount Sion is the gospel church. Christ is with his church, and in the midst of her in all her troubles, therefore she is not consumed. His presence secures perseverance. His people appear honourably. They have the name of God written in their foreheads; they make a bold and open profession of their faith in God and Christ, and this is followed by suitable actings. There were persons in the darkest times, who ventured and laid down their lives for the worship and truth of the gospel of Christ. They kept themselves clean from the wicked abominations of the followers of antichrist. Their hearts were right with God; and they were freely pardoned in Christ; he is glorified in them, and they in him. May it be our prayer, our endeavour, our ambition, to be found in this honourable company. Those who are really sanctified and justified are meant here, for no hypocrite, however plausible, can be accounted to be without fault before God. (Rev 14:6-13)
[Rev.14.6-Rev.14.13]
Verses 6-13
The progress of the Reformation appears to be here set forth. The four proclamations are plain in their meaning; that all Christians may be encouraged, in the time of trial, to be faithful to their Lord. The gospel is the great means whereby men are brought to fear God, and to give glory to him. The preaching of the everlasting gospel shakes the foundations of antichrist in the world, and hastens its downfal. If any persist in being subject to the beast, and in promoting his cause, they must expect to be for ever miserable in soul and body. The believer is to venture or suffer any thing in obeying the commandments of God, and professing the faith of Jesus. May God bestow this patience upon us. Observe the description of those that are and shall be blessed: such as die in the Lord; die in the cause of Christ, in a state of union with Christ; such as are found in Christ when death comes. They rest from all sin, temptation, sorrow, and persecution; for there the wicked cease from troubling, there the weary are at rest. Their works follow them: do not go before as their title, or purchase, but follow them as proofs of their having lived and died in the Lord: the remembrance of them will be pleasant, and the reward far above all their services and sufferings. This is made sure by the testimony of the Spirit, witnessing with their spirits, and the written word.
[Rev.14.14-Rev.14.20]
Verses 14-20
Warnings and judgments not having produced reformation, the sins of the nations are filled up, and they become ripe for judgments, represented by a harvest, an emblem which is used to signify the gathering of the righteous, when ripe for heaven, by the mercy of God. The harvest time is when the corn is ripe; when the believers are ripe for heaven, then the wheat of the earth shall be gathered into Christ's garner. And by a vintage. The enemies of Christ and his church are not destroyed, till by their sin they are ripe for ruin, and then he will spare them no longer. The wine-press is the wrath of God, some terrible calamity, probably the sword, shedding the blood of the wicked. The patience of God towards sinners, is the greatest miracle in the world; but, though lasting, it will not be everlasting; and ripeness in sin is a sure proof of judgment at hand.

The redeemed sing of God's holiness and deliverance (verses 1–4)

John saw seven angels in heaven preparing to carry out the last judgments.

Henry interprets their task as bringing the destruction of Antichrist to completion.

In his reading, Babylon's wickedness had reached its full measure, and therefore the time had come for God's full judgment against it.

Yet the scene also contains extraordinary consolation.

Believers still living amid the world's distress are like people standing upon a sea of glass mixed with fire.

They can look forward to their final deliverance even before it arrives.

Every new mercy they receive gives them reason to sing a new song of praise.

The more we discover of God's wonderful works, the more we will celebrate his greatness as the Lord God Almighty, Creator and Governor of all worlds.

But his title Emmanuel, King of the saints, makes him especially dear to those he has redeemed.

Anyone who understands God's power in judgment, the value of his favor and the glory of his holiness should worship him alone with deep reverence.

His praise rises above heaven and earth.

The angels receive the bowls of judgment (verses 5–8)

In judging Antichrist and those associated with that power, God fulfills the prophecies and promises of his word.

The angels are prepared for their work.

Their clean white clothing and golden bands across their chests symbolize the purity, holiness, righteousness and excellence of God's judgments.

They are ministers of divine justice and carry out their task without wrongdoing.

They receive the bowls containing God's righteous anger.

Even the weakest creature becomes irresistible when the Lord appoints it as the means of his judgment.

The angels receive the bowls from one of the four living creatures.

Henry interprets the living creature as representing a minister of the true church and regards the action as an answer to the prayers of God's servants and people.

He expects the removal of Antichrist to shake the entire world.

Even sincere believers might face confusion and suffering while that judgment unfolds.

God's greatest deliverances for the church sometimes come through awesome and astonishing acts of Providence.

The church will not enter its fully blessed condition until its stubborn enemies have been removed and halfhearted or merely formal Christians have been purified.

When everything contrary to Scripture has been cleansed away, the church will become spiritual, pure and united, firmly established in faithful worship and service.

Chapter 15
Chapter Outline
A song of praise is sung by the church. | (1-4) |
Seven angels with the seven plagues; and to them one of the living creatures gives seven golden vials full of the wrath of God. | (5-8) |
Verses 1-4
Seven angels appeared in heaven; prepared to finish the destruction of antichrist. As the measure of Babylon's sins was filled up, it finds the full measure of Divine wrath. While believers stand in this world, in times of trouble, as upon a sea of glass mingled with fire, they may look forward to their final deliverance, while new mercies call forth new hymns of praise. The more we know of God's wonderful works, the more we shall praise his greatness as the Lord God Almighty, the Creator and Ruler of all worlds; but his title of Emmanuel, the King of saints, will make him dear to us. Who that considers the power of God's wrath, the value of his favour, or the glory of his holiness, would refuse to fear and honour him alone? His praise is above heaven and earth.
[Rev.15.5-Rev.15.8]
Verses 5-8
In the judgments God executes upon antichrist and his followers, he fulfils the prophecies and promises of his word. These angels are prepared for their work, clothed with pure and white linen, their breasts girded with golden girdles, representing the holiness, and righteousness, and excellence of these dealings with men. They are ministers of Divine justice, and do every thing in a pure and holy manner. They were armed with the wrath of God against his enemies. Even the meanest creature, when armed with the anger of God, will be too hard for any man in the world. The angels received the vials from one of the four living creatures, one of the ministers of the true church, as in answer to the prayers of the ministers and people of God. Antichrist could not be destroyed without a great shock to all the world, and even the people of God would be in trouble and confusion while the great work was doing. The greatest deliverances of the church are brought about by awful and astonishing steps of Providence; and the happy state of the true church will not begin till obstinate enemies shall be destroyed, and lukewarm or formal Christians are purified. Then, whatever is against Scripture being purged away, the whole church shall be spiritual, and the whole being brought to purity, unity, and spirituality, shall be firmly established.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe first vial is poured out on the earth, the second on the sea, the third on the rivers and fountains.1–7The fourth on the sun, the fifth on the seat of the beast.8–11The sixth on the great river Euphrates.12–16And the seventh on the air, when shall follow the destruction of all antichristian enemies.17–21
The first three bowls and God's righteous judgment (verses 1–7)

We should pray that God's will may be done on earth as it is in heaven.

Here John sees a succession of terrible acts of divine Providence.

These judgments seem to recall the plagues of Egypt: similar sins are met by similar punishments.

Henry connects the seven bowls with the earlier seven trumpets, which he interprets as representing the rise of Antichrist.

In that reading, the downfall of the church's enemies resembles the manner in which their power first grew.

The earth, air, sea, rivers and cities associated with this wicked power are subjected to judgment.

The destruction expresses God's opposition to the evil in which that society had participated.

The angels witnessing and carrying out God's judgment praise his justice and truth.

They honor him for avenging his servants, whose persecutors had inflicted cruel suffering on the saints and prophets.

The fourth and fifth bowls: suffering without repentance (verses 8–11)

The human heart is so deeply corrupted that even the most severe misery does not by itself bring a sinner to repentance.

God's special grace is necessary.

Hell itself is filled with blasphemy.

People who understand human history, Scripture and their own hearts should know that suffering sometimes makes sinners more furious against God, even when they recognize his hand in their troubles.

Let sinners seek repentance through Christ and the renewing grace of the Holy Spirit now.

Otherwise, Henry warns, they will remain unhumbled and unrepentant, increasing guilt and misery through all eternity.

Darkness is the opposite of knowledge and wisdom.

It therefore pictures the confusion and folly of idolatrous followers of the beast.

Darkness also opposes pleasure and joy and thus pictures anguish and inward distress.

The sixth bowl: Euphrates, deception and watchfulness (verses 12–16)

Henry offers alternative possible interpretations of the drying of the Euphrates.

It probably symbolizes, in one reading, the destruction of Turkish power and idolatry, preparing a way for the return of the Jews.

In another reading, Babylon represents Rome under a symbolic name, because the city could not then be named openly.

In that case, the fall of Rome would also devastate the trade and resources on which its power depended.

Henry adds that perhaps an opening would follow for the Eastern nations to join Christ's church.

These are his tentative historical interpretations, not established identifications or a timetable supplied by the prophecy.

Before losing his power, the great dragon gathers his remaining forces for one desperate conflict.

God warns the church so that his people may prepare for severe trials and temptation.

Christ therefore calls his professed servants to watch, expect his sudden return, and avoid the shame of being found apostates or hypocrites.

Christians disagree about the dates and seasons of future events.

Yet on one essential point they agree: Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, will return suddenly to judge the world.

For people who live near him, that coming is a joyful hope.

They do not wish to postpone it.

The seventh bowl and Babylon's overthrow (verses 17–21)

When the seventh angel emptied his bowl, Babylon's destruction was completed.

The church triumphant in heaven saw it and rejoiced.

The church still struggling on earth saw its deliverance and could rejoice in victory.

God remembered the great and wicked city.

For a time he had seemed to overlook its idolatry and cruelty, but he had not forgotten.

Even things that had appeared most secure were carried away in the collapse.

Yet people continued to blaspheme.

The severest judgments cannot produce repentance without God's grace.

Indeed, becoming more stubborn against God in response to his righteous judgments is a sure warning of final destruction.

Chapter 16
Chapter Outline
The first vial is poured out on the earth, the second on the sea, the third on the rivers and fountains. | (1-7) |
The fourth on the sun, the fifth on the seat of the beast. | (8-11) |
The sixth on the great river Euphrates. | (12-16) |
And the seventh on the air, when shall follow the destruction of all antichristian enemies. | (17-21) |
Verses 1-7
We are to pray that the will of God may be done on earth as it is done in heaven. Here is a succession of terrible judgments of Providence; and there seems to be an allusion to several of the plagues of Egypt. The sins were alike, and so were the punishments. The vials refer to the seven trumpets, which represented the rise of antichrist; and the fall of the enemies of the church shall bear some resemblance to their rise. All things throughout their earth, their air, their sea, their rivers, their cities, all are condemned to ruin, all accursed for the wickedness of that people. No wonder that angels, who witness or execute the Divine vengeance on the obstinate haters of God, of Christ, and of holiness, praise his justice and truth; and adore his awful judgments, when he brings upon cruel persecutors the tortures they made his saints and prophets suffer.
[Rev.16.8-Rev.16.11]
Verses 8-11
The heart of man is so desperately wicked, that the most severe miseries never will bring any to repent, without the special grace of God. Hell itself is filled with blasphemies; and those are ignorant of the history of human nature, of the Bible, and of their own hearts, who do not know that the more men suffer, and the more plainly they see the hand of God in their sufferings, the more furiously they often rage against him. Let sinners now seek repentance from Christ, and the grace of the Holy Spirit, or they will have the anguish and horror of an unhumbled, impenitent, and desperate heart; thus adding to their guilt and misery through all eternity. Darkness is opposed to wisdom and knowledge, and forebodes the confusion and folly of the idolaters and followers of the beast. It is opposed to pleasure and joy, and signifies anguish and vexation of spirit.
[Rev.16.12-Rev.16.16]
Verses 12-16
This probably shows the destruction of the Turkish power, and of idolatry, and that a way will be made for the return of the Jews. Or, take it for Rome, as mystical Babylon, the name of Babylon being put for Rome, which was meant, but was not then to be directly named. When Rome is destroyed, her river and merchandise must suffer with her. And perhaps a way will be opened for the eastern nations to come into the church of Christ. The great dragon will collect all his forces, to make one desperate struggle before all be lost. God warns of this great trial, to engage his people to prepare for it. These will be times of great temptation; therefore Christ, by his apostle, calls on his professed servants to expect his sudden coming, and to watch that they might not be put to shame, as apostates or hypocrites. However Christians differ, as to their views of the times and seasons of events yet to be brought to pass, on this one point all are agreed, Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, will suddenly come again to judge the world. To those living near to Christ, it is an object of joyful hope and expectation, and delay is not desired by them.
[Rev.16.17-Rev.16.21]
Verses 17-21
The seventh and last angel poured forth his vial, and the downfal of Babylon was finished. The church triumphant in heaven saw it and rejoiced; the church in conflict on earth saw it and became triumphant. God remembered the great and wicked city; though for some time he seemed to have forgotten her idolatry and cruelty. All that was most secure was carried away by the ruin. Men blasphemed: the greatest judgments that can befal men, will not bring to repentance without the grace of God. To be hardened against God, by his righteous judgments, is a certain token of sure and utter destruction.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesOne of the angels who had the vials, explains the meaning of the former vision of the antichristian beast that was to reign 1260 years, and then to be destroyed.1–6And interprets the mystery of the woman, and the beast that had seven heads and ten horns.7–18
The woman on the scarlet beast (verses 1–6)

Henry identifies the woman with Rome, and more particularly interprets the symbols as pointing from pagan Rome toward what he calls papal Rome.

In his account, pagan Rome conquered and ruled mainly through military power, while allowing subject nations much of their previous religion and custom.

He accuses the later papal system of gaining and keeping power over kings and nations through political manipulation, deception, and promises of spiritual advantage.

This is Henry's historical Protestant polemical interpretation, not an identity conclusively settled by the text of Revelation or a statement about every Roman Catholic believer.

Worldly honor, riches, ceremony and pride appeal to minds governed by bodily desires and worldly ambitions.

Yet outward prosperity and splendor provide no security against God's judgment.

Henry understands the golden cup as a symbol of enticing appearances, deception and influence that lead others into idolatry and sin.

The woman is called the mother of prostitutes, picturing a power that trains others in false worship and wickedness.

She is also described as drunk with the blood of the saints and martyrs of Jesus, persecuting them without being satisfied.

Henry is horrified by the extraordinary quantities of Christian blood shed by people who called themselves Christians.

He believes such persecution gives solemn confirmation to the warnings found in biblical prophecy.

Do not be deceived by fashionable, profitable or outwardly magnificent religion.

Turn instead from the mystery of iniquity and study the great mystery of godliness.

Look to Christ's example and learn humility and thankfulness.

The more we resemble him, the less easily false religion deceives us.

The beast's heads, horns and final defeat (verses 7–14)

The beast “was, and is not, and yet is.”

In Henry's reading, the ancient form of pagan Roman idolatry and persecution had disappeared, yet another form of religious domination later revived similar patterns.

Those living within its influence would submit blindly to deception, except for the faithful remnant God had chosen.

The beast's seven heads were, in his interpretation, the seven hills of Rome and seven forms of government.

He explained the sequence as five already past, one existing when John wrote, and one still future.

In his polemical scheme, the papacy became an eighth ruling authority, restoring idolatry in a new form.

The ten horns represented ten kings whose kingdoms were yet to rise when John received the vision.

Henry associated them with kingdoms arising after the Roman Empire's breakup, temporarily supporting Rome's interests.

These are specific interpretive claims made by Henry, not a historical reconstruction independently established by the biblical text.

Whatever the details of those symbols, Christ must reign until every enemy is under his feet.

He wins because he is King of kings and Lord of lords, holding ultimate authority over every earthly and spiritual power.

His followers are called and equipped for faithful service and will remain loyal to him.

The rulers turn against the woman (verses 15–18)

God governs even the hearts and purposes of rulers.

Through his Providence they accomplish what he has foretold without intending to fulfill his plan.

The kings eventually discover their foolishness and how the woman had deceived and enslaved them.

They become instruments in her destruction.

Henry connects the great city that ruled kings in John's day with Rome.

In the final conflict, people who had united to commit wrongdoing turn upon one another with hatred and fury.

The wicked may become active agents of each other's downfall.

Believers, however, will be welcomed into the Lord's glory.

The Lord's people are his own portion.

His purposes stand firm, and he will accomplish all that pleases him, for his glory and the lasting happiness of those who serve him.

[Rev.17.1-Rev.17.6]
Chapter 17
Chapter Outline
One of the angels who had the vials, explains the meaning of the former vision of the antichristian beast that was to reign 1260 years, and then to be destroyed.
(1-6)
And interprets the mystery of the woman, and the beast that had seven heads and ten horns. | (7-18) |
Verses 1-6
Rome clearly appears to be meant in this chapter. Pagan Rome subdued and ruled with military power, not by art and flatteries. She left the nations in general to their ancient usages and worship. But it is well known that by crafty and politic management, with all kinds of deceit of unrighteousness, papal Rome has obtained and kept her rule over kings and nations. Here were allurements of worldly honour and riches, pomp and pride, suited to sensual and worldly minds. Prosperity, pomp, and splendour, feed the pride and lusts of the human heart, but are no security against the Divine vengeance. The golden cup represents the allurements, and delusions, by which this mystical Babylon has obtained and kept her influence, and seduced others to join her abominations. She is named, from her infamous practices, a mother of harlots; training them up to idolatry and all sorts of wickedness. She filled herself with the blood of the saints and martyrs of Jesus. She intoxicated herself with it; and it was so pleasant to her, that she never was satisfied. We cannot but wonder at the oceans of Christian blood shed by men called Christians; yet when we consider these prophecies, these awful deeds testify to the truth of the gospel. And let all beware of a splendid, gainful, or fashionable religion. Let us avoid the mysteries of iniquity, and study diligently the great mystery of godliness, that we may learn humility and gratitude from the example of Christ. The more we seek to resemble him, the less we shall be liable to be deceived by antichrist.
[Rev.17.7-Rev.17.14]
Verses 7-14
The beast on which the woman sat was, and is not, and yet is. It was a seat of idolatry and persecution, and is not; not in the ancient form, which was pagan: yet it is; it is truly the seat of idolatry and tyranny, though of another sort and form. It would deceive into stupid and blind submission all the inhabitants of the earth within its influence, except the remnant of the elect. This beast was seven heads, seven mountains, the seven hills on which Rome stands; and seven kings, seven sorts of government. Five were gone by when this prophecy was written; one was then in being; the other was yet to come. This beast, directed by the papacy, makes an eighth governor, and sets up idolatry again. It had ten horns, which are said to be ten kings who had as yet no kingdoms; they should not rise up till the Roman empire was broken; but should for a time be very zealous in her interest. Christ must reign till all enemies be put under his feet. The reason of the victory is, that he is the King of kings, and Lord of lords. He has supreme dominion and power over all things; all the powers of earth and hell are subject to his control. His followers are called to this warfare, are fitted for it, and will be faithful in it.
[Rev.17.15-Rev.17.18]
Verses 15-18
God so ruled the hearts of these kings, by his power over them, and by his providence, that they did those things, without intending it, which he purposed and foretold. They shall see their folly, and how they have been bewitched and enslaved by the harlot, and be made instruments in her destruction. She was that great city which reigned over the kings of the earth, when John had this vision; and every one knows Rome to be that city. Believers will be received to the glory of the Lord, when wicked men will be destroyed in a most awful manner; their joining together in sin, will be turned to hatred and rage, and they will eagerly assist in tormenting each other. But the Lord's portion is his people; his counsel shall stand, and he will do all his pleasure, to his glory, and the happiness of all his servants.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesAnother angel from heaven proclaims the fall of mystical Babylon.1–3A voice from heaven admonishes the people of God, lest they partake of her plagues.4–8The lamentations over her.9–19The church called upon to rejoice in her utter ruin.20–24
Babylon's fall and the call to come out (verses 1–8)

The downfall of mystical Babylon has been settled within God's purposes.

John sees another angel from heaven.

Henry suggests that the figure seems to be Christ himself, coming to defeat his enemies and spread the light of his gospel among the nations.

Babylon's wickedness is great.

It has abandoned true worship for idols, drawn people of all classes into spiritual unfaithfulness, and kept them loyal through wealth and luxury.

Henry understands the image as referring especially to spiritual commerce: people gaining riches by exploiting the sins, ignorance and foolishness of others.

God solemnly warns those who hope to receive mercy that they must come out of Babylon.

Henry also urges them to support its destruction, meaning the overthrow of the evil system depicted here.

There may be people who genuinely belong to God even within Babylon.

But his people must answer his call and separate from its wrongdoing.

Those who knowingly participate in the sins of the wicked expose themselves to the same judgments.

The kings and merchants mourn (verses 9–19)

Those mourning over Babylon have shared both its sensual pleasures and its commercial gains.

The kings of the earth were flattered into idolatry.

Henry accuses Babylon of permitting them to oppress their subjects so long as they remained obedient to her power.

The merchants profited, in his interpretation, by trading in indulgences, pardons and honors.

These observations express Henry's particular historical critique of what he regarded as the Roman Antichrist, not an identity the passage establishes beyond dispute.

Babylon's allies were willing to share her sinful pleasure and wealth, but not her punishment.

Their sorrow was purely worldly.

They did not grieve over God's anger against sin, only over their own lost conveniences.

This reveals the worldly spirit Henry associates with Antichrist.

The splendor and riches of wicked people will not protect them when judgment comes; they may even make the loss harder to bear.

The passage speaks of enslaved people and human souls as commodities.

Henry connects these images with destructive spiritual commerce that brought ruin to countless souls.

He explicitly observes that such wrongdoing is not limited to the system he identifies with Rome.

Successful merchants everywhere should therefore learn to seek the unsearchable riches of Jesus Christ alongside their earthly work.

Otherwise, riches may fly away even before death, leaving the desired pleasures gone.

In any case, death will soon end all their trade.

Without reconciliation to God, worldly wealth will be exchanged for the coffin and the worm, and the fire that cannot be quenched.

Heaven rejoices at the end of oppression (verses 20–24)

The same deliverance that makes God's servants rejoice on earth also brings rejoicing to the angels in heaven.

Henry expects even the apostles—whose memory he says was honored at Rome in ways he judged idolatrous—to rejoice in the fall of Babylon.

This is part of his historically situated Protestant reading of the passage.

Babylon's destruction reveals God's justice.

Because her fall is final, the persecuting power will never again trouble the faithful.

The vision supplies a sign assuring them of this complete end.

Let us learn from the errors and sins that brought others to ruin.

Recognizing how unstable all earthly possessions and institutions are, set your affections on things above.
classic_reading:
[Rev.18.1-Rev.18.8]
Chapter 18
Chapter Outline
Another angel from heaven proclaims the fall of mystical Babylon. | (1-3) |
A voice from heaven admonishes the people of God, lest they partake of her plagues. | (4-8) |
The lamentations over her. | (9-19) |
The church called upon to rejoice in her utter ruin. | (20-24) |
Verses 1-8
The downfal and destruction of the mystical Babylon are determined in the counsels of God. Another angel comes from heaven. This seems to be Christ himself, coming to destroy his enemies, and to shed abroad the light of his gospel through all nations. The wickedness of this Babylon was very great; she had forsaken the true God, and set up idols, and had drawn all sorts of men into spiritual adultery, and by her wealth and luxury kept them in her interest. The spiritual merchandise, by which multitudes have wickedly lived in wealth, by the sins and follies of mankind, seems principally intended. Fair warning is given to all that expect mercy from God, that they should not only come out of this Babylon, but assist in her destruction. God may have a people even in Babylon. But God's people shall be called out of Babylon, and called effectually, while those that partake with wicked men in their sins, must receive of their plagues. (Rev 18:9-19)
[Rev.18.9-Rev.18.19]
Verses 9-19
The mourners had shared Babylon's sensual pleasures, and gained by her wealth and trade. The kings of the earth, whom she flattered into idolatry, allowing them to be tyrannical over their subjects, while obedient to her; and the merchants, those who trafficked for her indulgences, pardons, and honours; these mourn. Babylon's friends partook her sinful pleasures and profits, but are not willing to share her plagues. The spirit of antichrist is a worldly spirit, and that sorrow is a mere worldly sorrow; they do not lament for the anger of God, but for the loss of outward comforts. The magnificence and riches of the ungodly will avail them nothing, but will render the vengeance harder to be borne. The spiritual merchandise is here alluded to, when not only slaves, but the souls of men, are mentioned as articles of commerce, to the destroying the souls of millions. Nor has this been peculiar to the Roman antichrist, and only her guilt. But let prosperous traders learn, with all their gains, to get the unsearchable riches of Christ; otherwise; even in this life, they may have to mourn that riches make to themselves wings and fly away, and that all the fruits their souls lusted after, are departed from them. Death, at any rate, will soon end their commerce, and all the riches of the ungodly will be exchanged, not only for the coffin and the worm, but for the fire that cannot be quenched.
[Rev.18.20-Rev.18.24]
Verses 20-24
That which is matter of rejoicing to the servants of God on earth, is matter of rejoicing to the angels in heaven. The apostles, who are honoured and daily worshipped at Rome in an idolatrous manner, will rejoice in her fall. The fall of Babylon was an act of God's justice. And because it was a final ruin, this enemy should never molest them any more; of this they were assured by a sign. Let us take warning from the things which brought others to destruction, and let us set our affections on things above, when we consider the changeable nature of earthly things.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe church in heaven and that on earth triumph, and praise the Lord for his righteous judgments.1–10A vision of Christ going forth to destroy the beast and his armies.11–21
The church praises God and the marriage of the Lamb is announced (verses 1–10)

When we praise God for mercies already received, we also express confidence and desire for the blessings yet to come.

Heavenly angels and redeemed people join in this triumphant song.

Christ is the Bridegroom of the church he has redeemed. Their glorious union will be complete in heaven.

Henry also suggests that the beginning of the millennium—which he describes as a thousand-year reign of Christ, or an era of happiness upon earth—can be understood as the celebration of their marriage here on earth.

In that happy condition, Christ's church will be purified from errors, divisions and corruptions in its doctrine, discipline, worship and conduct.

The Lord will then openly acknowledge her as his beloved and his delight.

Her clothing is not the bright and ostentatious display of the mother of prostitutes.

Instead, she wears clean, white linen: Christ's righteousness credited to her for justification and given to her in sanctification.

The marriage feast consists of God's trustworthy gospel promises, made plain, applied and sealed to believers by the Holy Spirit through the appointed ordinances.

Henry understands this as pointing to abundant grace and comfort for Christians in the happier days still to come.

When John tried to honor the angel religiously, the angel refused and directed him to worship God alone.

Henry applies that refusal against worship directed to bread and wine, saints or angels.

He also rejects worship given to Christ by those who deny that he is truly God by nature, because religious worship belongs to God alone.

The God who speaks truth here is the One worthy of worship, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Christ defeats the beast and its armies (verses 11–21)

Christ appears as the glorious Head of his church, riding a white horse—a sign of righteousness and holiness.

He wears many crowns because he is King of kings and Lord of lords.

His garment is portrayed as dipped in blood.

Henry connects this both with Christ's own blood, through which he purchased his mediatorial authority, and with the blood of the enemies over whom he triumphs.

He is called the Word of God.

No creature can comprehend the full glory of this name.

Yet Scripture tells us what we need to know: the Word is God revealed in human flesh.

The angels and saints who follow him share his purity and righteousness.

He now carries out the judgments foretold in the written word against those who resist him.

His royal name declares his rightful authority and warns even the greatest earthly rulers to submit to him.

Otherwise they must fall.

Every power of earth and hell may join the struggle, but none can defeat him.

These verses concern weighty events announced by God's prophets.

Those who followed wicked leaders will not be excused simply because they obeyed orders.

What a useless defense it will be on the day of judgment to say, “We merely followed our leaders and did what other people did.”

God has given us his word as the rule of life.

Neither the conduct of the majority nor the orders of powerful people can justify disobeying it.

Those who blindly follow the multitude in sin will go where that multitude goes, Henry warns: into the burning lake.
classic_reading:
[Rev.19.1-Rev.19.10]
Chapter 19
Chapter Outline
The church in heaven and that on earth triumph, and praise the Lord for his righteous judgments.
(1-10)
A vision of Christ going forth to destroy the beast and his armies.
(11-21)
Verses 1-10
Praising God for what we have, is praying for what is yet further to be done for us. There is harmony between the angels and the saints in this triumphant song. Christ is the Bridegroom of his ransomed church. This second union will be completed in heaven; but the beginning of the glorious millennium (by which is meant a reign of Christ, or a state of happiness, for a thousand years on earth) may be considered as the celebration of his espousals on earth. Then the church of Christ, being purified from errors, divisions, and corruptions, in doctrine, discipline, worship, and practice, will be made ready to be publicly owned by him as his delight and his beloved. The church appeared; not in the gay, gaudy dress of the mother of harlots, but in fine linen, clean and white. In the robes of Christ's righteousness, imputed for justification, and imparted for sanctification. The promises of the gospel, the true sayings of God, opened, applied, and sealed by the Spirit of God, in holy ordinances, are the marriage-feast. This seems to refer to the abundant grace and consolation Christians will receive in the happy days which are to come. The apostle offered honour to the angel. The angel refused it. He directed the apostle to the true and only object of religious worship; to worship God, and him alone. This plainly condemns the practice of those who worship the elements of bread and wine, and saints, and angels; and of those who do not believe that Christ is truly and by nature God, yet pay him a sort of worship. They stand convicted of idolatry by a messenger from heaven. These are the true sayings of God; of Him who is to be worshipped, as one with the Father and the Holy Spirit.
[Rev.19.11-Rev.19.21]
Verses 11-21
Christ, the glorious Head of the church, is described as on a white horse, the emblem of justice and holiness. He has many crowns, for he is King of kings, and Lord of lords. He is arrayed in a vesture dipped in his own blood, by which he purchased his power as Mediator; and in the blood of his enemies, over whom he always prevails. His name is "The Word of God;" a name none fully knows but himself; only this we know, that this Word was God manifest in the flesh; but his perfections cannot be fully understood by any creature. Angels and saints follow, and are like Christ in their armour of purity and righteousness. The threatenings of the written word he is going to execute on his enemies. The ensigns of his authority are his name; asserting his authority and power, warning the most powerful princes to submit, or they must fall before him. The powers of earth and hell make their utmost effort. These verses declare important events, foretold by the prophets. These persons were not excused because they did what their leaders bade them. How vain will be the plea of many sinners at the great day! We followed our guides; we did as we saw others do! God has given a rule to walk by, in his word; neither the example of the most, nor of the chief, must influence us contrary thereto: if we do as the most do, we must go where the most go, even into the burning lake.

Satan is restrained (verses 1–3)

The vision uses a figure to show the restraint placed upon Satan himself.

Through his almighty power, Christ will prevent the devil from misleading humanity as he has previously done.

Christ always possesses both the power and the means to break Satan's influence.

He shuts the prison by his power and seals it by his authority.

The church will enjoy a time of peace and prosperity.

Yet all her trials will not be over.

The first resurrection and the reign of the saints (verses 4–6)

The saints reign during the same period in which Satan is bound.

Those who suffer with Christ will reign with him in his spiritual and heavenly kingdom, reflecting his wisdom, righteousness and holiness.

Henry identifies this with the first resurrection, a blessing reserved for those who truly serve Christ and suffer for his sake.

Only holy people can be truly blessed, and everyone made holy will ultimately share that blessing.

We know something of the first death, and it is deeply frightening.

We have never directly experienced the second death, but it is more dreadful still: the soul's eternal separation from God.

May we never know it.

Those who share in a spiritual resurrection are delivered from its power.

Henry expects that after the destruction of antichristian, idolatrous and persecuting powers, a thousand years will come in which pure Christianity—right teaching, worship and holiness—will spread throughout the earth.

Through the almighty work of the Holy Spirit, fallen human beings will be made new.

Faith and holiness will then become as widespread as unbelief and wickedness appear to be now.

Imagine how many diseases, hardships and cruelties might disappear if all people became sincere and consistent Christians.

Public and private conflicts would cease, and happiness would increase in countless ways.

People would seek to relieve others' distress instead of increasing it.

We should pray for those promised days and do everything our public or private responsibilities allow to prepare the way for them.

Satan is released and the last conflict comes (verses 7–10)

While the present world remains, Satan's power will not be altogether destroyed, even when his activity has been restrained.

As soon as he is released, he returns to deceiving the nations and stirring them to war against God's saints and servants.

Would that Christ's ministers and people were as energetic and persistent in doing good as the enemies of his kingdom are in doing evil.

But God himself will fight the final and decisive battle for his people.

The victory will be complete, and all its glory will belong to him.

The final resurrection and judgment (verses 11–15)

After the events just foretold, the end approaches swiftly.

The vision mentions nothing else before Christ appears to judge the world.

On that great day, the Lord Jesus Christ will be seen in the majesty and terror of the Judge.

All the dead must stand before him: small and great, young and old, low and high, poor and rich.

No one is too insignificant to have gifts and duties to account for.

No one is important enough to escape the accounting.

The judgment includes not only those alive at Christ's return but everyone who has died.

A book of remembrance records good and evil.

The hidden book of each sinner's conscience will also be opened.

Actions long forgotten will be recalled.

Another book is Scripture, the rule by which human lives are judged.

The opening of the book of life also shows the Lord's knowledge of his people and his recognition of their repentance, faith and good works, revealing the blessings of the new covenant.

People will be judged according to their works, because their conduct reveals the principles that governed them.

Those whom the gospel has justified and acquitted will be recognized as justified and acquitted by the Judge.

They enter everlasting life without any further fear of death, hell or wicked enemies.

All these enemies are destroyed.

The second death is the final separation of sinners from God.

Our urgent concern should be to examine whether Scripture now confirms or condemns the way we live.

Christ will one day judge humanity's secrets according to the gospel.

Who could endure that judgment without his mercy?

[Rev.20.1-Rev.20.3]
Chapter 20
Chapter Outline
Satan is bound for a thousand years. | (1-3) |
The first resurrection; those are blessed that have part therein. | (4-6) |
Satan loosed, Gog and Magog. | (7-10) |
The last and general resurrection. | (11-15) |
Verses 1-3
Here is a vision, showing by a figure the restraints laid on Satan himself. Christ, with Almighty power, will keep the devil from deceiving mankind as he has hitherto done. He never wants power and instruments to break the power of Satan. Christ shuts by his power, and seals by his authority. The church shall have a time of peace and prosperity, but all her trials are not yet over.
[Rev.20.4-Rev.20.6]
Verses 4-6
Here is an account of the reign of the saints, for the same space of time as Satan is bound. Those who suffer with Christ, shall reign with him in his spiritual and heavenly kingdom, in conformity to him in his wisdom, righteousness, and holiness: this is called the first resurrection, with which none but those who serve Christ, and suffer for him, shall be favoured. The happiness of these servants of God is declared. None can be blessed but those that are holy; and all that are holy shall be blessed. We know something thing of what the first death is, and it is very awful; but we know not what this second death is. It must be much more dreadful; it is the death of the soul, eternal separation from God. May we never know what it is: those who have been made partakers of a spiritual resurrection, are saved from the power of the second death. We may expect that a thousand years will follow the destruction of the antichristian, idolatrous, persecuting powers, during which pure Christianity, in doctrine, worship, and holiness, will be made known over all the earth. By the all-powerful working of the Holy Spirit, fallen man will be new-created; and faith and holiness will as certainly prevail, as unbelief and unholiness now do. We may easily perceive what a variety of dreadful pains, diseases, and other calamities would cease, if all men were true and consistent Christians. All the evils of public and private contests would be ended, and happiness of every kind largely increased. Every man would try to lighten suffering, instead of adding to the sorrows around him. It is our duty to pray for the promised glorious days, and to do every thing in our public and private stations which can prepare for them.
[Rev.20.7-Rev.20.10]
Verses 7-10
While this world lasts, Satan's power in it will not be wholly destroyed, though it may be limited and lessened. No sooner is Satan let loose, than he again begins deceiving the nations, and stirring them up to make war with the saints and servants of God. It would be well if the servants and ministers of Christ were as active and persevering in doing good, as his enemies in doing mischief. God will fight this last and decisive battle for his people, that the victory may be complete, and the glory be to himself.
[Rev.20.11-Rev.20.15]
Verses 11-15
After the events just foretold, the end will speedily come; and there is no mention of any thing else, before the appearing of Christ to judge the world. This will be the great day: the Judge, the Lord Jesus Christ, will then put on majesty and terror. The persons to be judged are the dead, small and great; young and old, low and high, poor and rich. None are so mean, but they have some talents to account for; and none so great, as to avoid having to account for them. Not only those alive at the coming of Christ, but all the dead. There is a book of remembrance both for good and bad: and the book of the sinner's conscience, though formerly secret, will then be opened. Every man will recollect all his past actions, though he had long forgotten many of them. Another book shall be opened, the book of the Scriptures, the rule of life; it represents the Lord's knowledge of his people, and his declaring their repentance, faith, and good works; showing the blessings of the new covenant. By their works men shall be justified or condemned; he will try their principles by their practices. Those justified and acquitted by the gospel, shall be justified and acquitted by the Judge, and shall enter into eternal life, having nothing more to fear from death, or hell, or wicked men; for these are all destroyed together. This is the second death; it is the final separation of sinners from God. Let it be our great concern to see whether our Bibles justify or condemn us now; for Christ will judge the secrets of all men according to the gospel. Who shall dwell with devouring flames?
